_comment: Beginner hints for phase 01, rewritten as a ladder in plain words: hint 1 says what the checks want and the idea that gets you there; hint 2 names the exact tool with a tiny example. The app adds a third, 'the shape of an answer', from the solution. ex_lib.dump applies these over the authored hints and fails on an unknown id.
p01.001: The checks call `greet("Ada")` and compare what comes back with the text `Hello, Ada!`. So your function has to build that text and hand it back with `return`. `print` only shows text on the screen - the function would give back `None` and every check would fail.
To put the name inside the text, use an f-string: `f"Hello, {name}!"`. The part in braces is replaced by whatever `name` holds, so `return f"Hello, {name}!"` is the whole body.
p01.002: Turn the formula into Python one piece at a time: take `celsius`, multiply it by 9, divide by 5, then add 32 - and `return` the result.
Write it as `celsius * 9 / 5 + 32`. Use `/`, not `//`: `//` throws away the fraction, so 36.6 degrees would come out wrong.
p01.003: Work from the smallest unit up: first split the seconds into whole minutes plus leftover seconds, then split those minutes into whole hours plus leftover minutes.
`divmod(a, b)` gives both parts of a division at once: `divmod(3661, 60)` is `(61, 1)` - 61 whole minutes, 1 second left. Do it again with the minutes and 60, then `return hours, minutes, seconds`.
p01.004: Break the name into words, take the first letter of each, make it a capital and put a dot after it, then glue the pieces together.

`full_name.split()` (with nothing in the brackets) splits on any amount of space and never gives empty words. For each word, `word[0].upper() + "."`, and `"".join(...)` glues the pieces with nothing between them.
p01.005: An f-string can do more than insert a value: after a colon inside the braces you can say how to format the number - separators, decimals and so on.
`f"{amount:,.2f}"` adds thousands commas (`,`) and exactly two decimals (`.2f`). Put the dollar sign in front: `f"${amount:,.2f}"`.
p01.006: Deal with bad input first: if the score is below 0 or above 100, `raise ValueError(...)`. Then check the grades from the top down, so each test only needs one number.
`if not 0 <= score <= 100: raise ValueError("out of range")`, then `if score >= 90: return "A"`, then `>= 80` for B, and so on, with `return "F"` at the end for everything left.
p01.007: Say the rule out loud as a chain: divisible by 4, and at the same time either not a century, or a century divisible by 400. That whole sentence is one True/False expression.
`x % n == 0` means "x divides evenly by n". The rule is `year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)` - the brackets matter.
p01.008: Keep a running total that starts at 0, then go through the numbers 1, 2, 3 ... up to n and add each one to it. Return the total at the end.
`range(1, n + 1)` gives 1 up to n - the stop number itself is left out, so add one. Set `total = 0` before the loop (not inside it) and do `total += value` inside.
p01.009: Make an empty list, loop over 1 to n, decide what each number becomes, and append it. The order of the tests matters: a multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 3 and 5.
Test `value % 15 == 0` first, then `% 3`, then `% 5`, with `else` appending the number itself. If you test 3 first, 15 becomes "Fizz" and never reaches "FizzBuzz".
p01.010: Duplicates are the trap: in `[5, 1, 5, 3]` the second largest value is 3, not 5. Remove repeats first, then look at what is left.
`sorted(set(numbers))` removes repeats and sorts smallest to largest. If that has fewer than 2 values return `None`; otherwise `[-2]` is the second from the end.
p01.011: A list comprehension builds a new list in one line: for every number, keep it only if it is even, and put its square in the new list.
The shape is `[what_to_put for item in items if condition]`. Here: `[n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]` - `n % 2 == 0` means n is even.
p01.012: Handle the no-answer cases first (shorter than 3, or an even length) by returning `""`. Then find the middle position and take one character either side of it.
The middle index is `len(text) // 2`. A slice `text[start:stop]` stops before `stop`, so the three middle characters are `text[middle - 1:middle + 2]`.
p01.013: Three jobs in order: throw away the extra spaces (outside and inside), then capitalise each word.
`name.split()` gives the words with every run of space removed; `" ".join(...)` puts them back with single spaces; `.title()` capitalises each word. They chain: `" ".join(name.split()).title()`.
p01.014: Split the phrase into words, take the first letter of each, make it a capital, and join the letters with nothing between them.
`phrase.split()` gives the words. `"".join(word[0].upper() for word in phrase.split())` does the rest in one line.
p01.015: Lower-case the text, split it into words, and keep a dictionary of counts: for each word, add one to its count - starting from 0 the first time you see it.
`counts.get(word, 0)` returns the count so far, or 0 for a new word, so `counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1` works for both. Once yours passes, look at `collections.Counter`.
p01.016: Two cases: the key is in the dictionary, or it is not. Test which one first, then return the right thing for each.

`if key in data:` checks the keys (not the values). Return `data[key]` there, and `default` otherwise. Do not write `if data[key]:` - that crashes on a missing key and wrongly treats 0 or "" as missing.
p01.017: Walk the list once. Remember what you have already kept; keep an item only the first time you meet it. A set is the fast way to remember, a list keeps the order.
Start with `seen = set()` and `out = []`. For each item: `if item not in seen:` add it to `seen` and `out.append(item)`. Return `out`.
p01.018: `sorted` can sort by anything you choose: give it a small function that turns each name into what it should be sorted by - surname first, then first name.

`name.rpartition(" ")` splits at the last space: `"Ada Lovelace"` gives `("Ada", " ", "Lovelace")`. Return `(last, first)` from the key function and call `sorted(names, key=key)` - it makes a new list.
p01.019: Sort the names by score, highest first, with ties going alphabetically, then take the first n.
Sort `scores.items()` with `key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0])` - a minus sign flips the score so the highest comes first, and the name breaks ties. Then take `[:n]` and keep just the names.
p01.020: Go through the list with each item's position, and keep the position whenever the item equals the target.
`enumerate(items)` gives `(index, item)` pairs. `[i for i, item in enumerate(items) if item == target]` collects the positions in one line.
p01.021: Walk the two lists side by side, pairing the first name with the first score and so on, and build a dictionary from the pairs.
`zip(names, scores)` pairs them up and stops at the shorter list - exactly the rule you need. `dict(zip(names, scores))` turns the pairs into a dictionary.
p01.022: Start with an empty dictionary. For each row, add its amount to the running total for its category, starting from 0 for a category you have not seen.
`out[key] = out.get(key, 0) + row["amount"]` handles both new and known categories, where `key = row["category"]`.
p01.023: A default like `basket=[]` is made once, when the function is defined, and then shared by every call - that is why items leak between calls. The fix is to make a new list inside the function each time.
Use `basket=None` as the default, then `if basket is None: basket = []` as the first line of the body. A caller who passes their own list still gets theirs.
p01.024: `*values` collects the positional arguments into a tuple and `**options` collects the keyword ones into a dictionary. Build the count part first; if there are no options, you are done.
`head = f"{len(values)} values"`. For the options, sort their names and format each as `key=value`: `" ".join(f"{k}={options[k]}" for k in sorted(options))`, then `f"{head} | {tail}"`.
p01.025: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. It needs a stopping case that answers directly - otherwise it never ends and you get a RecursionError.
Raise `ValueError` for negative n, return 1 when n is 0 or 1, and otherwise `return n * factorial(n - 1)`.
p01.026: Try the division; if Python raises an error because b is zero, catch that error and return `None` instead of crashing.
`try: return a / b` then `except ZeroDivisionError: return None`. Name the exact error - a bare `except:` would also hide real bugs.
p01.027: Three checks, in order: is it a type you accept (a string or a number, but not True/False)? Can it become a whole number? Is it between 0 and 130? Raise the matching error as soon as one fails.
`isinstance(value, (str, int, float))` checks the type - `bool` counts as an int, so exclude it. Wrap `int(value)` in `try` and turn a failure into `ValueError`, then check `0 <= age <= 130`.
p01.028: Go through the values one at a time and try to convert each. If one fails, skip it and carry on with the next - the loop must keep going.
Put the `try` inside the loop around `out.append(int(value))`, and `except (TypeError, ValueError): continue`. `int("x")` raises ValueError; `int(None)` raises TypeError.
p01.029: Open the file, go through it line by line, and count the lines that still have something in them after you remove the spaces.
`with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:` opens the file and closes it for you. `for line in fh:` gives each line, and `if line.strip():` is true only when something other than whitespace is there.
p01.030: `save` writes the dictionary into the file as JSON text; `load` reads that text back into a dictionary. Open the file for writing in one and for reading in the other.
In `save`: `with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh: json.dump(data, fh)`. In `load`: open it normally and `return json.load(fh)`. Remember `import json` at the top.
p01.031: Turn both strings into real dates, subtract one from the other, and take the number of days - positive either way round.
`date.fromisoformat("2026-01-31")` reads the string (after `from datetime import date`). Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta; `.days` is the number of days, and `abs(...)` makes it positive.
p01.032: Count only the letters, ignoring case. Then pick the letter with the highest count, and on a tie the one that comes first in the alphabet. No letters at all means `None`.

`Counter(ch for ch in text.lower() if ch.isalpha())` counts the letters (after `from collections import Counter`). `min(counts, key=lambda ch: (-counts[ch], ch))` picks the most common, breaking ties alphabetically.
p01.033: Python has two built-ins for exactly these questions: one asks "is this true for every item?", the other "is it true for at least one?".
`all(n > 0 for n in numbers)` and `any(n < 0 for n in numbers)`. `all` of an empty list is True, which is what the task asks for.
p01.034: First clean the text: keep only letters and digits, in lower case. Then a palindrome reads the same backwards as forwards.
`"".join(ch.lower() for ch in text if ch.isalnum())` cleans it. `cleaned[::-1]` is the text reversed, so return `cleaned == cleaned[::-1]`.
p01.035: Build a new dictionary where each old value becomes a key and each old key becomes its value. If two keys share a value, the later one simply overwrites the earlier.
A dictionary comprehension does it in one line: `{value: key for key, value in mapping.items()}`.
p01.036: Keep one running total. For each number, add it to the total and append the total so far to the result list.
Set `total = 0` and `out = []` before the loop; inside, `total += number` then `out.append(total)`. When it passes, compare with `itertools.accumulate`.
